I don't know why it should be true, but the devices that use wired hubs are the most reliable at staying connected - Hue, SmartThings/Samsung, Aeotec - they chug right along, running their routines. They're only ever a problem when it's time to reset them, and then you need John Titor level ancient devices to get deep into your 2.4gHz network without making an executive decision to jump to 5 gHz during set up, but that's another story for another day).

Anyway - the devices that use wired hubs work better and more reliably. So I have a bunch of hubs connected to my router. The router has to be out in the great wide open. Otherwise, it does not route. It has what's supposed to be an attractive design, right? Yeah, when it's got a bunch of different colored cables sticking out of it, not so much. It looks like I used to look taking my kid to school drop off.

Flat black cables run smoothly and nearly invisibly against the black cabinet the router sits on. There's plenty of bandwidth, and the hubs don't have to be noticeable to work.

Negative space for the win.

text_fidelity_a:
FiiO X5 High Resolution Music Player (2nd Generation)(Titanium) I love my FiiO X5 2nd gen player! I love that it has two micro SD card slots (which I use both for a total of 192GB of storage space, with one 64GB card and one 128GB card), because I can put two separate sets of music in there and go back and forth between the cards depending on my musical needs (for example, on the 64GB card, I put recently purchased tracks, and for the entirety of my rest of my library, I put those tracks on the 128GB card). It allows me faster access to my newer stuff, which I want to listen to now, vs. randomizing the rest of my music from the other card.

The sound is unheard of (ha ha, sorry for the pun). Nothing compares to the quality of sound that comes out of this little machine, for its size and price. Pair it with a set of high quality hi-fi headphones and some FLAC music files, and you've got yourself an insane little music machine. You'll never go back to Apple or another brand of music player. You'll find yourself hooking it up to your home sound system and playing all of your music through it. I can't say enough for the sound quality. You WILL notice a difference between crummy .mp3 files and other low-quality sound files. You WILL find yourself craving FLAC files, and you will go wherever you can to find them. You might even start converting your entire CD music collection into FLAC, even though you'd already converted them all to .mp3. You WILL find yourself hoping that someday soon, Amazon will start offering FLAC files instead of .mp3s! (HINT HINT NUDGE NUDGE!) ;) Seriously, though, you probably haven't realized how GOOD your music will sound until you listen to it on this FiiO X5 2nd gen. Even the .mp3s sound better. Especially if you use noise cancelling headphones.

I like that you can adjust the configuration and tell it which buttons to remain active when the screen is off, depending on your preferences. I also like that there are several preset themes to choose from. The screen is easy to read and nicely displays album art.

The unit itself has a wonderful weight to it given the aluminum shell. The volume wheel moves easily and there is a slight tactile feedback click. That wheel controls both the song volume and song selection, depending on which screen you're on when you use it. The power on button has a tiny LED light that's blue when it's running and red when it's charging. There are volume up/down buttons beneath the power button and those buttons are some of the buttons that you can choose whether or not to have active while the screen is off.

I'm not sure if I there's a firmware update that needs to be done that could change this, but there are a couple of things that are pretty bothersome in general about this unit:

1) There is no way to search for a song. If, like me, you have more than 5,000 songs, it's impossible to sit and scroll through each album/folder to find a specific song. I suppose if you're some kind of major organization guru (which I thought I was, but apparently not at this), it would be possible to arrange your music folders into genres or some other category to make it easier to get to the exact music you need to play, but if you've moved over from iTunes like I have, you're probably real spoiled with the ability to view songs either by artist, album, song name, etc., as well as the ability to do a search. Here, you're pretty much on your own, depending on how you've got your music library set up. Having purchased most of my music here on Amazon, it's all arranged by artist name in individual folders. I have several hundred folders set up like this, and scrolling through everything with that scroll wheel can take a very, very long time to find the one thing you're looking for.

2) The unit can be quite SLOW to respond to your clicks. It is not touch-screen, and when you click on a button to change tracks forward/backward or to change from looking at what's playing into another option, such as a list of the songs on the album, it can be quite sluggish. Again, if you're used to using an iPod, you'll be frustrated with the lack of responsiveness of this unit. Again, I keep hoping a firmware update will come out that addresses this.

3) Whenever you add music to your micro SD card(s) [NOTE: There is NO onboard storage, it's purely on whatever card(s) you insert into it] you have to completely update your whole media library. This can take a long time depending on how much music you have, so keep this in mind and don't expect to add music and listen to it immediately. In other words, plan ahead for this :)

4) It's not as user friendly as the typical Apple products you may be used to. You'll get used to it, but don't expect the polished feel because of issues like #1 and #2, above.

5) Playlists are not straightforward. Yes, you can be playing a song and add it to a playlist that resides on one of your SD cards. However, importing playlists can be tricky and you may find yourself looking to the internet to help convert your existing playlists from your prior player. Expect to spend some time on this unless you're totally okay with starting over from scratch (I wasn't okay with this). Also, any playlists that you save to your SD card that you've hand-converted do not show up as a playlist on the FiiO. Instead, you have to navigate to the file on your player as if you were looking for a song, and play it as if you were playing a song. Only playlists you've created on the machine show up in the Playlist section, not playlists you've brought in from elsewhere. There is no 'import' feature or anything fancy like that, so you're pretty much on your own unless you add a song one at a time to Playlist 1, Playlist 2, etc. (I do not yet see a way to rename these as there is no keyboard function on this machine, so you're stuck with those names).

I think with time, the FiiO's software will catch up closer to what you're seeing from the high-visibility media consumer based music players, but right now with this X5 you should be more concerned with how WONDERFUL your music sounds vs the issues associated with the frumpy software that comes with it.
text_fidelity_b: FiiO X5 High Resolution Music Player (2nd Generation)(Titanium)

text_fidelity_a:
WD My Net AC1300 HD Dual Band Router Wireless AC WiFi Router Accelerate HD UPDATE: Since the review below this paragraph, I have put this up without a backup, and it's been a fire and forget mission. No problems with wireless network service. My "OK" review still stands, but I'm still optimistic some firmware upgrades or a big "that's it!" on my end could get everything working better or even flawlessly.

I have an extensive wired gigabit network in my home, so it has not been my top priority to replace my antiquated wireless B/G router (although I do use it much for casual surfing, mind you). Because I've been very busy when at home lately and in no mood to deal with nuisance computer/network issues, I put this new router in parallel with the old so that if issues came up, I wouldn't have to deal with them immediately. After about three weeks, albeit with only casual and sporadic "trying to make it work right", it's still not ready to run solo, obviously reason enough to just rate average.

This is unfortunate because it has a lot of cool touted features. The funny thing is when I was first setting it up I was thinking how they really have it idiot-proofed - even the WAN port is color coded to the included network cable (they don't even call it a WAN port, BTW).

But as is so often the case, by trying to make something useable to the masses, it actually becomes more difficult for advanced users to do simple tasks: I sort of want some Network Attached Storage (NAS), but have been too cheap/lazy/power misery to want to bother dealing with it, so I thought it would be great to try this router with its USB ports - ideally, I was going to put some hard drives in my gun safe, which is beside my telecom closet, and attach them to the router via USB, and have them both set to turn off when not in use. But it's just not working. I could go into a rant here about how Windows tries to set up a GUI so that people ignorant to computers can access their media when I all I really want to do is access the root of the drives and then do what I want without interference, but I'll save you my usual rant because I don't want you to misinterpret that it is indeed the router's fault that it rarely recognizes my attached devices (although interaction with various versions of Windows is the fault of both companies). The fact is, from the router's access page, you can see that my drives are often not recognized at all, or the router still thinks I have something attached that I've detached a while back (and sometimes even after a reboot). Clearly, I'm not about to put these drives down in a safe on another floor; it's easier just to deal with them locally. I was unable to EVER access these from a tablet or a phone; I wasn't about to waste that much time when I couldn't even rely on it to work with decent Windows machines.

The gigabit Ethernet ports are a great feature, and the wireless portion works better, but there have been a few times where I've checked my machines and they've reverted back to my legacy network, meaning that the new router obviously went down, if only for a short time. Thus, I'm not ready to put this machine up solo and deal with any headaches that I may have to incur.

With some cool features like QoS (Quality of Service) and port forwarding, etc., it sounds like it could be a great router. I can't begin to test these well when I'm still frustrated with making it look like a real seamless network. These are probably things that can and will be fixed with firmware updates, but they should have had this ironed out before release. If I hear of a good update, I'll give it another go if I'm still interested and will let you know how it works out.
text_fidelity_b: WD My Net AC1300 HD Dual Band Router Wireless AC WiFi Router Accelerate HD

Canon EF-S 55-250mm F4-5.6 IS STM Lens with UV Protection Filter - 58 mm I purchased this lens on Amazon offered by a gray market vendor for $140 (new!). Gray Market means there is no USA Warranty. I haven't tried to see if it is eligible, but I assume it would not be. As of this writing (10/12/2014), that vendor, CD Supply, is still offering the lens - though now for $170. Still an incredible deal for this lens which came new in the standard Canon box with manual etc. (If it isn't warranteed - I can buy another and still be about the price of just one at regular price).

The lens itself: I was pleasantly surprised. I could have purchased it in my kit with the 70D camera, but wasn't really interested. For $140 - what the heck. The photos are sharper than from the kit 18-135mm STM IS lens in my opinion (and that's a pretty decent lens as kit lenses go). It is very small and light weight for a pretty long lens - especially on a crop sensor.
BONUS: Macro. It actually can get pretty decent magnification. Something like 1/4:1 from a pretty good distance at 250mm.
Plus it works great with extension tubes. I've used it with 12mm and 26mm (not together) and it worked great. Even autofocus - though I wouldn't recommend that for Macro.

Negatives (though - again - if you get it for cheap, these are quibbles):
- No lens hood provided. Buy a knock off on Amazon for $13
- Not a super bright lens. You're going to need some decent sunlight or a good flash with this. It ramps up to f/5 minimum pretty quick and f/5.6 not too long after that. Only the widest shots will get F/4.
- Pretty cheaply built (but it's a cheap lens!)

text_fidelity_a:
Ring Video Doorbell Pro – Upgraded, with added security features and a sleek design (existing doorbell wiring required) Great Addition to Home Security System

First I should say there is no 100% perfect home security system. That is why I have a home security “solution” that incorporates several different, but tied together systems. I have a full Lorex Camera System, Smart Things Hub and a wired alarm system. But even with all that there was something missing. If I wasn’t home, all of the other items were only good after the fact. Meaning I could see who was at my door, or in my house after I got back home. Sure I could set alerts on those other devices, but when your phone chirps 10 alerts per hour, it just becomes white noise. These other systems had so many false positives I ultimately turned them off.

Pros: But the Ring Bell filled several voids in these other systems. One, the false positives are almost nonexistent due to the ability to mask the alert area of the camera. My existing security system may alert me, but then I had to log into the camera system to see what was going on. The time it takes to do that could make a real difference. The ability to answer and interact with someone who rings your bell from your couch or from at work is invaluable! The person ringing the bell has no idea where you are answering from. But the best part is being able to ignore solicitors and screen people before you answer. It’s as easy as answering a phone call and the live image is instantaneous. The fact that it integrates with my SmartThings hub is just icing on the cake.

I was able to install the Ring Bell Pro in about 15 minutes following the simple instructions. It is extremely well thought out. The video quality of the Ring Pro is excellent! It does not have a very wide angle and there is a slight fisheye distortion, but it should be more than sufficient for most applications. The mobile app is also very intuitive. As I mentioned, when you get an alert, you can immediately see who is at the door and you can choose to answer and speak, or just watch.

Cons: I was confused by the wall plate not having the mounting holes line up with the existing wall plate holes. This required drilling holes above and below the existing holes to mount the plate. I could see no reason for this.

The unit can easily be ripped off the wall with one hand. Because the main unit mounts onto a plastic wall cover, it would take about 2 seconds to remove and disable the unit. But at least you will get an alert and when you went to log in you would know something was wrong. However, the Ring Pro has a unique purchase protection that sates “If your Ring™ Video Doorbell is stolen at any time after your purchase, Bot Home Automation, Inc. will replace your Ring™ Video Doorbell at no charge to you”. That’s pretty impressive!

If you want to keep your Ring History, you have to sign up for their paid service. Otherwise you only see live views. Prices vary by plan, but they do offer one free month for new customers.

Overall: There is no perfect security system. Each one has its plusses and minuses. But the Ring Pro should be part of every home security solution. Also, if I had to choose only one component for a complete home security solution, this would be high up on my list.

Update: 7/10/2017 - The unit has powered down several times and gone off line. This has required disconnecting it at the unit or the bell inside and reconnecting it. I have verified my power supply works OK. We will see if this becomes a ongoing issue.

Update: 10/30/2017 - I have downgraded from 5 to 3 starts today. First, the unit still stops working at times and needs to be rebooted by disconnecting the wires at the bell. The existing analog bell only chimes for the Ding and not the Dong. However the biggest disappointment is a inherent design flaw in the phone application. If someone come to the door and quickly goes away, like the UPS guy, by the time you take out your phone, open the app and connect, they are long gone. So you do get alerted, but there is no way to access the app fast enough to get a live view of what happened. You have to wait a few minutes until you can review the past activity, which requires a subscription. I guess it's still better than nothing.
text_fidelity_b: Ring Video Doorbell Pro – Upgraded, with added security features and a sleek design (existing doorbell wiring required)

text_fidelity_a:
HUION Inspiroy H1060P Graphics Drawing Tablet with 8192 Pressure Sensitivity Battery-Free Stylus and 12 Customized Hot Keys, 10 x 6.25 inches Digital Art Tablet for Mac, Windows PC and Android *UPDATED*
After a year of use. The tablet canvas started chipping in the middle of the protective coating. Stylus pressure and positioning still work but it's annoying as heck plus not it's even chipping more every time I go over same spot. I've never had that happen with any of the Huion & Wacom tablets I've owned for more years than this. I also can't seem to find a tablet protector for this either. So kind of bummed because I really like this...or want to really like this tablet.

*Original review*
First off, just like Wacoms these Huions are compatible with literally all major art software programs as well as budget programs.
I personally have used this Huion with Photoshop, Illustrator, 3D Studio Max, Zbrush, Mudbox, 3D Coat, Substance Painter, Clip Art Studio (Manga Studio), Krita, Painter, Paint Too Sai....can't remember the rest.
This NEW HUION 1060 PLUS is ASIN# B01FTE9HS2 and it comes with a stylus holder, 4 stylus nibs, a carrying case and drawing glove.
There is also another NEW version I saw on Amazon which includes 10 stylus nibs, holder and a glove without carrying case but they are the same exact tablet. They are both the same price on Amazon as of this writing.
Not to get you confused but there is an older one also called the 1060 Plus but it is not labled NEW or UPGRADED.
It is different cosmetically and has older technology and features.
The NEW 1060 Plus has Full-Area Surface Cover and Thinner Border, which makes the drawing surface bigger plus an attached side holder for stylus. Also, Quieter Express Keys, Better Linearity in art programs, Better pen pressure sensitivity.
(Specifications: Resolution: 5080 LPI, Report Rate: 233 RPS, 2048 Levels of Pressure, 10" x 6.25" active area.)
*Note: I just found out they released an even newer one with smoother pressure/linearity and has 8192 levels of pressure but it costs a little bit more.*

Now to the good stuff. Drivers were easy to install and worked right away; which is surprising because I've had driver issues with every non-Wacom tablets in the past. Actually, there are rare hiccups where the USB wouldn't recognize the tablet so I just have to replug back in. I've even had that issue with wacoms so I would just have to reconnect the USB back in to get it to recognize. Another common issue with older tablets (even Wacom) is that with Photoshop sometimes doesn't register the pressure sensitivity so I would have to either restart Photoshop or reconnect the USB.
But other than the super rare hiccups, this tablet looks very professional and is an great upgrade from the Huion H610 Pro, which I own, plus the Huion GT 220 graphics tablet which similar to the Wacom 22HD but way better IPS picture quality. I own the Wacom 22HD Touch and is totally not worth the $2000 I spent compared to the $700 I bought the Huion GT220 for. The Huion GT220 may have not come with express keys but I never use those awkward positioned keys anyways. I prefer the keyboard or game pad. I also owned a Wacom Intuos 2, Wacom Intuos 4 and an Intuos 4 Wireless which I've used throughout my professional career as an artist. (I wanted to compare them to see if a lower cost alternative is worth the savings). But my recommendation is if you are already an artist or aspiring to be an artist, don't hesitate on getting the tablet that gives you the best bang for your buck. Wacom does have good build but drivers can be flakey too. I've had some Wacoms stop recognizing the drivers to the point where I have to reinstall it.
With the 1060 PLUS you're pretty much set with a drawing tablet if you can't afford a Wacom or Surface Pro for all your 3D, drawing and painting needs. And to me, the pressure curve and sensitivity is feels equal to, if not better than, the Wacom tablets.

This Huion is the best bang for you buck for aspiring artist that want a professional tablet at the best price. I don't want to stray anyone away from a Wacom if they can afford it. But it's great to know that you can now save 1/5 the cost of a Wacom with the similar, if not better, specifications.
Actually, I purchased 5 of these for us artists at work and also had to recently recommend this Huion to my friends and family looking for a tablet for their kids that are also aspiring artist and animators. They showed me their kids' drawings and animation with the mouse I convinced their parents to get a drawing tablet. It is a must have for artists but you don't need to spend an arm and a leg. I truly believe this is the best $80 price range tablet on the market today that runs on Windows 10 (as of this writing). It has worked well for me for my professional (and personal) work with 3D sculpting, drawing and painting. Sorry Wacom....$250 to $300 for a comparable mid-size tablet is not aspiring artist friendly. They may look a bit cooler but they all achieve the same end. They also have Wacom Bamboos or budget Wacoms under $70 but they all lack the pressure sensitivity and features with only 1024 levels of sensitivity. I'm not a Huion salesman but this just makes sense and achieves the same end.....which is quality art without frustrating hardware and features.
text_fidelity_b: HUION Inspiroy H1060P Graphics Drawing Tablet with 8192 Pressure Sensitivity Battery-Free Stylus and 12 Customized Hot Keys, 10 x 6.25 inches Digital Art Tablet for Mac, Windows PC and Android

text_fidelity_a:
Plantronics BackBeat PRO Wireless Noise Canceling Hi-Fi Headphones with Mic - Compatible with iPhone, iPad, Android, and Other Smart Devices I would, that I could give these headphones a zero-star rating. As I don’t think they deserve a whole star. When I was in school, a gold star meant something. And these headphones are not deserving of such.
Ok, on with the bad. My first set of these. If I would whipe the sweat out of my left ear. Left ear specifically, as the right ear did not produce this effect. The sound would cut off. Not the little off, then on again. As the phones shut off when you take them off your head. So a little off then on, would be expected. But I mean off, and stay that way. Then you need to turn off the headphones, with the switch, and back on again.
Which leads to the second problem. The phones cannot reconnect after the connection has been broken. The computer will blue screen, and restart. I thought, well maybe it is the Bluetooth receiver. So I got a new one, by a different company. Same issue.
Problem three. None of the buttons work. The buttons I am referring to are the play, pause, track forward, or track backward.
And it really makes me sad, to say these bad things about these phones. And I really tried to blame something other things at fault, to save their face. Because they have the most awesome form factor I can find in a headphone. The buttons are so intuitively placed, even if they do not work. The design, is obviously a different department. And the volume, is not controlled by a buttons. But rather a good old analog type knob. And the sound quality is pretty good, and also the noise cancelling works.
Oh yeah, I almost forgot. Because I really like the form factor. I thought I should give them another chance. So I replaced this set, with another set of the same model. And had the same problems. Evey, single, one, of them.
text_fidelity_b: Plantronics BackBeat PRO Wireless Noise Canceling Hi-Fi Headphones with Mic - Compatible with iPhone, iPad, Android, and Other Smart Devices

text_fidelity_a: Rankie DisplayPort (DP) to HDMI Adapter, 4K Resolution Ready Converter with Audio (Black) I would have given this five stars, except that 1) I purchased it July 23, 2016 and 2) on October 1, 2016, it failed.  I'd noticed that my monitor was extremely susceptible to static interference, where my other two monitors (not using this adapter) were not.  Tonight it just quit working altogether.  I checked the connections on the back of the monitor, all were fine.  I then checked the connection to the graphics card (NVidia gtx 1060), which is what I used this adapter for.  Unfortunately, when I attempted to pull the adapter out of the graphics card, the adapter came apart in pieces, leaving the end part in the HDMI port in the graphics card.  I've attached photos to show.  I could not take the piece out of the graphics card with my bare hands.  I had to completely shut down my computer and use pliers, held on each side (left and right side, as top/bottom pinch type grip didn't work), and pull with all of my might to remove the piece out of the computer.  I couldn't believe this thing.  I will never use this product again and suggest you find a product with a more reliable name/more reliability in general.  I hope this port on my graphics card isn't destroyed!!!!
text_fidelity_b: Rankie DisplayPort (DP) to HDMI Adapter, 4K Resolution Ready Converter with Audio (Black)

This flash drive is USB-C only, which is great for me. No need to find an adapter to plug it into a USB-C port (or Thunderbolt, on a Mac). It also works with Android phones, though you will need to remove any phone case, as the USB-C connector is too short to reach through a case.

The flash drive is tiny! The body and cap are slick and smooth, so it can be hard to grip the lid. The lid does not fasten onto the back, so it’s super easy to lose. The lid does have a small hole for a lanyard loop, and so does the body of the flash drive. But I still feel like looks were valued over function for the lid and body design.

On the 64GB model, the write speeds are *up* to 300 MB/s. I actually timed moving about 760MB worth of files to the drive, and it took 72 seconds.
text_fidelity_b: SAMSUNG Type-C™ USB Flash Drive, 64GB, Transfers 4GB Files in 15 Secs w/Up to 300MB/s 3.13 Read Speeds, Compatible w/USB 3.0/2.0, Waterproof, 2022,Blue

Images are in color with more flexibility the Kindle reader on my Mac and I guess that's what I expected, only smaller. If I were only reading fiction, and image quality was not important I would probably keep it rather than go through the hassle of returning it.

As a technical writer I cannot imagine creating such an unfriendly and unwieldy interface. Opened the box less than an hour ago and the "user manual" on the Kindle evidently doesn't have a way to exit the manual or even get back to the the beginning without endlessly pressing the left side of the screen one screen page at a time. Worse yet after after endless "left tapping" I am getting close to the beginning of the manual I am taken forward again to a chapter near the end of the manual. Insane! I just want to get out of the manual or at least access the tool bar and am unable to do so . Supposedly tapping the top of the page allows access to the tool bar but all that does is highlight a word at the top of the page. What's up with this? So far extremely disappointed and frustrated. Nothing should be this difficult. While writing this review the screen changed to the cover and blurb of a book and the Kindle is frozen on that page. By the way, image is dark as is the entire page. It just keeps getting better, folks. Hopefully a restart will remove the kinks and won't be a total waste of money, time and effort. If not this is Kindle is useless and going back. Recently, though, as it reached six years of age, it started being unreliable when playing it, so I finally gave in and bought a new one. This time around I ordered the 4GB model. I really wanted to get the dark pink color again, but it wasn't offered here on Amazon, so I got the purple color called "indigo." It is much darker than the picture. It looks almost black, and the back side of the device actually is black. However, it is an attractive color.

This updated version has a lot more features than my old Sansa Clip. I probably will never use every feature it offers, but I am extremely happy to have quadrupled my storage space, and the sound quality is much better.

The on/off switch is on the top right, instead of the left side, and where the on/off switch used to be on my old Sansa Clip, on the left side, is where the volume switch is on this model. Until I figured that out, I had accidentally muted the device.

I am hoping to figure out soon how to download WMA audiobook files from my local library onto this device. One of the prime uses I have for an MP3 player like this one is listening to audiobooks when exercising or doing chores around the house.

So far, I am really happy with this new version of a beloved device.

Garmin nüvi 1350LMT 4.3-Inch Portable GPS Navigator (Discontinued by Manufacturer)) I drive in and around the Boston area, where none of the streets run north/south or east/west, every other intersection is a rotary, and a wrong turn down a one way street can take you an hour to correct.

The Nuvi is slightly better than trying to drive with a map on your steering wheel. I have been using mine for awhile now, and it mostly gets me where I want to go.

The problem is mostly how it does it. As many have already noted, there is no easy way to get it to show you alternate routes. And out of the city, especially, the route it gives you can be full of surprises. Take you off the highway and onto a dirt road for no reason whatsoever surprises. That happened to my husband on his way to a job in Hartford.

And forget trying to get around traffic. I was using it to get home from a doctor's office and saw that there was a ton of traffic on the route it was giving me through Harvard Square, so I turned toward another way home - one I do not know as well, but I know it is possible to get home that way - expecting the Nuvi to tell me it was recalculating and give me my next turn.

It did so, and I turned and followed the directions each time as it - get this - took me into the Harvard Business School parking lot and then out onto a one way street that put me on a no-turning-back 100% committed course to the traffic in Harvard Square.

Thanks, Nuvi.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin nüvi 1350LMT 4.3-Inch Portable GPS Navigator (Discontinued by Manufacturer))

TP-LINK TL-PA511 KIT AV500 Powerline Gigabit Adapter Starter Kit, up to 500Mbps I wish I would have tried these a long time ago. Could have saved me a lot of aggravation over the years. I'm sure a lot of people have heard of these and are likely sceptical. At least that's my excuse. That and I live in an old house with old wiring and many circuits. It's a San Francisco Victorian with bent hallways and a nightmare for both cell reception and WiFi range.

I have wanted to get networking from the back of the flat to the front. That seemingly simple concept never works. What I did get to work was to put WiFi in the back, and then a WiFi extender in the front with a 20' antenna extension which then pushed the antenna to the middle. Even that was tricky.

I even once tried a Verizon 4G LTE router to get some broadband in the front. It was expensive and still didn't work. So I pretty much resigned myself to just running cat5e or cat6 cable down the hallway, which is what I wanted to avoid. But right before I did that I decided to give this a shot.

The install took all of 5 seconds, seriously. Plug a box into one outlet in the back of the flat. Plug that box into my switch. Now run to the front of the flat. Plug that box into an outlet. Run the Ethernet from that box to my switch. Plug Linux box into switch. Boot up and test the speed. 53 MB/sec down, 4 up. Pretty much my ISP limit. My only concern is security, but they do have software, but it requires Windows I bet. I use Linux. I'll see what I can do to lock this down. But it does work. Fantastically so. Not sure the front and back are on the same circuit. Guessing they are. Either way, I finally got the front connected to the back without WiFi or a long Ethernet running down my hallway. And that is 5 stars!
text_fidelity_b: TP-LINK TL-PA511 KIT AV500 Powerline Gigabit Adapter Starter Kit, up to 500Mbps
